note: USB 2.0 board layout, return paths and reference planes, decoupling and PDN. Extracted 2026-10-27; quotes checked by tools/library_quotes.py. Ott's and Archambeault's positions are cited as reported by the CompuPhase paper, not from their own texts.

claims.statement: USB 2.0 DP/DM run as a 90 ohm differential pair (about 45 ohm single-ended); the tolerance quoted differs by vendor (+/-10 %, +/-15 %, or +5/-10 ohm).

citations.locator: Appendix A, Table A-1 p.16 (same row in Tables A-2..A-8)
citations.quote: USB2.0 DP/DM pair differential impedance 81 90 99 Ω
Trace Impedance 90Ω ±15% differential, 45Ω ±15% single ended
Control the differential impedance (Zdiff) of the DP/DM signals to 90 ... +5/-10
citations.note: The ohm signs (90 ohm, +5/-10 ohm) are missing from the PDF text layer.

citations.quote: Control the single-ended characteristic impedance (Z0) of USB signals to between 40 ... and 55
citations.note: The ohm signs (40 ohm, 55 ohm) are missing from the PDF text layer.

enforced_by: intent impedance (compiled to the DIFF_HS class)
claims.note: Tolerance band is the only disagreement; 90 ohm nominal is unanimous. A checker should use the tightest (Microchip 80-95 ohm) as a warning band and +/-15 % as the failure band.

claims.statement: The two members of a USB 2.0 high-speed pair differ in routed length by no more than about 1.25 mm (50 mil), with any matching meander placed near the end where the mismatch arises.

citations.quote: Skew within any USB2.0 differential pair 50 Mils
Each member of a High-Speed differential pair should be no more than 1.25 mm (50 mil) longer than the other member.
add serpentine routing to match the lengths as close to the mismatched ends as possible
add serpentine routing to match the lengths as close to the mismatched ends as possible
Add any need serpentines very near where the length error is introduced into the line.

claims.could_enforce: per-pair |len(DP) - len(DM)| from the routed board, compared with max_length_mismatch_mm
claims.note: 50 mil = 1.27 mm; Microchip rounds to 1.25 mm. At full speed (12 Mbit/s) this is very loose; it matters for 480 Mbit/s.

claims.statement: Total USB 2.0 trace length from device to connector stays below 12000 mil (304.8 mm).

citations.quote: USB2.0 Tracelength (total) 4000 12000 Mils
keep total trace length for signal pairs to a minimum

claims.note: The table has MIN/TYP/MAX columns but only two numbers; 4000 mil probably sits in TYP and 12000 in MAX. Reading 4000 as a minimum would make no physical sense.

claims.statement: USB 2.0 high-speed traces longer than about 150 mm may significantly degrade signal quality.

citations.quote: High Speed signal traces longer than ~15 cm (~6 in), and SS traces longer than ~10 cm (4”) may significantly degrade signal quality.

claims.note: Factor-of-two disagreement with TI (305 mm). Irrelevant to small boards like easy2350 where the pair is a few cm; matters for hubs and board-to-board runs.

claims.statement: Each USB 2.0 data trace has at most 4 vias, preferably none, and both members of the pair have the same number of vias at matching positions.

citations.quote: Number of vias allowed on each USB2.0 differential trace (total) 4 Vias
Minimize the number of vias used and balance the number and placement of them between the signals within the pair if used.
ensure that the via count on each member of the differential pair is equal and that the vias are as equally spaced as possible
designers must take into account the length of the vias when verifying parameters such as inter pair skew

claims.statement: USB data pairs carry no stubs and no test points or probe pads; components on the line sit in-line, not on a branch.

citations.quote: Number of stubs allowed on any USB differential pair trace (total) 0 Stubs
Do not place probe or test points on any high-speed differential signal.
minimize stubs on high speed traces to reduce increased insertion loss
All of the USB traces must be routed as differential pairs. Avoid using any stubs on these lines.

claims.could_enforce: net topology check: USB nets are a single chain pad-to-pad (no T-junctions, no test-point footprints)

claims.statement: USB 2.0 pairs keep at least 0.762 mm (30 mil) from any other signal and at least 1.27 mm (50 mil) from clocks and periodic signals.

citations.quote: maintain a minimum keep-out area of 30 mils to any other signal throughout the length of the trace
USB differential pair to clock or high-speed periodic signal trace spacing 50 Mils
increase this keep-out to a minimum of 50 mils to maintain proper isolation

claims.could_enforce: KiCad netclass clearance for the USB pair (constraint compiler)

claims.statement: USB 2.0 pairs keep a gap of at least 3x the larger of trace width and dielectric height to every signal outside the pair.

citations.quote: Maintain a routing spacing (gap) of at least 3X between High-Speed USB signals (DP and DM) to the signals outside of the USB pair.
define this gap in terms of either the USB trace width or the dielectric height between the signal and its reference plane, whichever is greater

claims.could_enforce: clearance_mm against 3*max(w, h) using the stackup
claims.note: On a 1 mm 2-layer board (h ~ 1 mm, w = 0.8 mm per rp2350.usb.impedance) this demands ~3 mm, versus TI's fixed 0.76 mm. The scaled rule is physically better grounded (crosstalk scales with h) but the two disagree by 4x on exactly the boards this project makes.

claims.statement: USB pairs are not routed under or near crystals, oscillators, switching regulators, magnetics, mounting holes or clock-generating ICs.

citations.quote: Do not route high-speed traces under or near crystals, oscillators, clock signal generators, switching power regulators, mounting holes, magnetic devices
Do not route high-speed traces under or near crystals, oscillators, clock signal generators, switching power regulators
Avoid placing or routing noisy circuits near the sensitive RBIAS resistor ... the crystal circuit, and the USB differential pair signals.

claims.could_enforce: router keep-out regions around crystal/regulator/magnetics footprints for USB nets; no numeric distance given (use signal.usb2.spacing_* as minimum)

claims.statement: USB ESD/EMI protection sits as close as possible to the connector, with flow-through pinout preferred, and unprotected traces kept away from protected ones.

citations.quote: Place ESD and EMI protection devices as close as possible to the connector.
TI recommends selecting devices that permit flow-through routing of the USB differential signal pair
Keep any unprotected traces away from protected traces to minimize EMI coupling.
Place any ESD devices for the USB lines near the USB connectors.

claims.note: TI also asks for 60 % reference-plane voids under ESD signal pads (§3.14 p.15); that targets SuperSpeed losses and is not carried as a USB 2.0 rule here.

claims.statement: A through-hole USB receptacle is fed from the layer opposite its body so the pin is not a stub; an SMT receptacle is fed on its own layer without vias.

citations.quote: Making these connections on the bottom layer of the PCB prevents the through-hole pin from acting as a stub
make high-speed differential signal connections on the top layer. Making these connections on the top layer eliminates the need for vias
Transmission line characteristics of surface mount (SMT) USB connectors are easiest to control.

claims.could_enforce: layer of the last segment entering each USB connector pad vs the connector's mounting side

claims.statement: A differential pair runs together and symmetrically; asymmetric segments at package escape and connector entry are as short as possible, with breakout within 6.35 mm (0.25 in) of the package.

citations.quote: These deviations must be as short as possible and package break-out must occur within 0.25 inches of the package.
package break-out must occur within 0.25 inches of the package

claims.could_enforce: length of uncoupled (pair gap > target) segments per pair; first coupled point within max_breakout_mm of the pad
claims.note: The RP2350 reference boards' chip-side escape (pin to 27 ohm resistor, ~4 mm) falls inside this allowance.

claims.statement: High-speed signals reference a solid ground plane; a power plane is not used as their reference unless unavoidable, and then only with AC caps and ground vias for the return.

citations.quote: TI does not recommend high-speed signal references to power planes.
If unavoidable, use AC coupling capacitors and ground vias to allow the return signal to have a path back

claims.statement: USB and other critical signals may reference either an unbroken power plane or an unbroken ground plane.

citations.quote: Route critical signals over unbroken reference (power or ground) planes.
Route USB differential signals over unbroken reference (power or ground) planes.
always have a ground plane or power plane on the layer above or below a signal layer

claims.note: TI SLLA414 §3.4 says ground-or-power, then §3.5 says power only if unavoidable; TI is inconsistent with itself as well as with Microchip. Settle by simulation: same pair over GND vs over VDD with the decoupling as placed.

claims.statement: A high-speed track never crosses a split or void in its reference plane; every millimetre has the reference directly beneath it.

citations.quote: High-speed signals should be routed over a solid GND reference plane and not across a plane split or a void in the reference plane
the return path must take a longer route than the signal path
Always consider the ground return path for each critical signal.

claims.statement: If a high-speed track must cross a plane split, a stitching capacitor of at most 1 uF bridges the split as close as possible to the crossing.

citations.quote: These capacitors should be 1 µF or lower and placed as close as possible to the plane crossing.
These capacitors should be 1µF or lower and placed as close as possible to the plane crossing.

claims.could_enforce: for each split crossing, distance from crossing point to nearest capacitor bridging the two planes

claims.statement: High-speed differential tracks stay at least 2.29 mm (90 mil) from the edge of their reference plane and at least 1.5 trace widths from any void in it.

citations.quote: Ensure that high-speed differential signals are routed ≥ 90 mils from the edge of the reference plane.
routed at least 1.5 W (calculated trace-width × 1.5) away from voids in the reference plane
Verify that high-speed differential signals are routed ≥ 90 mils from the edge of the reference plane.
SuperSpeed signal traces should not be within 5X trace width of the reference plane edge or of the splits

claims.could_enforce: extend unreferenced_length_mm: count length whose reference copper does not extend max(1.5 W, edge rule) beyond the track on both sides
claims.note: TI exempts voids under SMD pads it deliberately clears. Microchip's 5W rule is stated for SuperSpeed only.

claims.statement: A high-speed track keeps one ground reference from source to sink where possible; where it must change layer and therefore reference plane, ground stitching vias tie the two ground planes within 5.08 mm (200 mil) of the signal via, placed symmetrically; closer is better.

citations.quote: Place these stitching vias symmetrically within 200 mils (center-to-center, closer is better) of the signal transition vias.
via-stitch both GND planes together to maintain continuous grounding and uniform impedance
If vias are necessary for any SuperSpeed signals, add complementary ground vias.
The entirety of any high-speed signal trace should maintain the same GND reference from origination to termination.
Do not change the reference plane of the high speed signal trace unless completely unavoidable.

claims.could_enforce: for each signal via on a high-speed net, distance to nearest GND via (center to center)
claims.note: 200 mil is generous for 480 Mbit/s rise times on a thin board; it is TI's ceiling, not a target.

claims.statement: Ground floods on different layers are joined with multiple vias, and every narrow ground flood ends in a via at each corner and end so it carries return current instead of resonating.

citations.quote: Connect ground floods on different layers with multiple vias and ensure narrow ground floods are terminated with a via at all flood corners and ends.
For two-layer structures, flood the bottom layer with ground.

claims.could_enforce: for each GND copper island: via count >= 2 and every pour 'finger' narrower than N mm has a via within M mm of its tip (dangling-copper check)
claims.note: Directly relevant to 2-layer boards like the RP2350 minimal reference, where the bottom flood is the only reference.

claims.statement: Decoupling capacitor vias sit in or immediately beside the capacitor pads with short, wide connections, because trace length adds roughly 6-12 nH/cm in series with the capacitor.

citations.quote: place vias from the planes as close as possible to the pad of the capacitor. Preferably, they should be incorporated into the copper structure
Common PCB traces have self-inductances that measure between 6 nH and 12 nH per centimeter.
Place bypass vias within or as close as possible to the bypass capacitor pad.
Use via-in-pads for capacitors.

claims.note: SLOA069 p.10: 'Even a couple of millimeters ... adds 1.2 nH'. decoupling_path_mm measures pin-to-cap distance; the via-to-pad distance on the ground side is not yet measured.

claims.statement: Each bypass capacitor's ground (and ideally supply) connection uses more than one via; bulk capacitors use at least two vias to each of power and ground.

citations.quote: Use multiple ground vias per capacitor to divide the effect of the fanout trace’s and via’s impedances
For system bulk large value capacitors, use at least two vias to connect to power & ground.
Placing multiple inductors in parallel can reduce inductance.

claims.note: SLOA069 p.11: a 0.4 mm via through 1.5 mm board is ~1.1 nH; via height dominates, so on a 2-layer 1.6 mm board each via is ~1 nH.

claims.statement: Bypass capacitors go on the same side as the IC they serve; on the far side the intervening vias add inductance and make them less effective.

citations.quote: These capacitors are usually less effective if they are placed on the bottom of the PCB because of the intervening via inductances.

claims.could_enforce: side(cap) == side(served IC) for decoupling parts in the intent
claims.note: Single source. SLOA069 p.9 mentions bottom-side placement only as one of several bad options for DIP packages. Check against how the RP2350 reference boards place theirs before promoting.

claims.statement: Supply current is routed from the rail to the capacitor pad first and then to the IC pin, so any feed trace/via inductance sits before the capacitor rather than in its loop.

citations.quote: the power signal originates at the voltage rail source, then to the capacitor, then to the Hub Controller pin
the via and trace inductances appear before the capacitor, which is on the same pad as the power pin of the IC

claims.could_enforce: topology check on the supply net: rail via/trace joins at the capacitor pad, and the cap-to-pin segment carries no other branch

claims.statement: Bypass capacitors use small packages (0402 or smaller) and X7R-class or better dielectric, not Y5V/Z5U.

citations.quote: MLCC capacitors of 0402 size or less have lower parasitic inductance and fit closer to the hub device pins
Use capacitors with appropriate temperature coefficients (Ex., X7R -- not Y5V).
Select capacitors with small footprint to minimize ESL.

claims.could_enforce: package and dielectric fields on decoupling parts (ccomp check package)
claims.note: SLOA069 p.7 goes further ('High-frequency decoupling requires NPO/COG capacitors') for RF op-amp work; impractical for digital rails and not taken as a rule. Bogatin (MLCC section) notes ESL is set by body size and mounting, not by value.

claims.statement: Several capacitor values in parallel (for example 100 nF with 10 nF or 100 pF) cover different frequency bands, each value aimed at its own self-resonance.

citations.quote: No single capacitor can be expected to properly decouple a system where multiple RF frequencies are present.
two or more capacitors may be required to properly bypass. Each capacitor is then targeted at a different frequency range.
[Archambeault 2002] recommends to always place two capacitors in parallel: one of 100nF and one of 100pF, in order to break the resonance.

claims.note: SLOA069 is written for RF/high-speed op-amps (e.g. a 1.9 GHz example), not digital PDNs.

claims.statement: With MLCCs, parallel decoupling capacitors of one value avoid the anti-resonance peaks that mixed values create between their self-resonances; mixing values is legacy practice from leaded capacitors.

requirement.measured_example: two 100 nF 0402 in parallel beat 100 nF + 10 nF 0402 near 50 MHz (CompuPhase VNA, 1 MHz-1 GHz)

citations.locator: section 'MLCC Capacitors and the Myth of the High-Frequency Capacitor'
citations.quote: A 10 and 0.1 uF MLCC capacitor will have exactly the same high frequency impedance.
When three different value capacitors with the same ESL are combined in parallel, two parallel resonance peaks are generated between their self-resonant frequencies.
mixing capacitor types for decoupling may well be counter-productive
test [5] improves on test [4] only in the area around 100MHz, while it performs significantly worse around 50MHz
[Ott 2009] recommends putting two capacitors in parallel, but in contrast to Archambeault he asserts that both should be identical

claims.could_enforce: slow-tier PDN impedance sweep of the rail with the placed caps: report peak |Z| between lowest and highest SRF
claims.note: Bogatin et al. also say neither strategy is proven robust without system-level analysis ('they both may be equally acceptable, equally marginal'). CompuPhase notes anti-resonance does not create noise, it only fails to suppress it at that frequency. Good candidate for the simulation tier.

claims.statement: When only one capacitor serves a pin, use the highest capacitance available in the smallest practical body at the needed voltage rating, rather than a small 'high-frequency' value.

citations.quote: If only one capacitor is specified on a pin ... always use the highest capacitance allowed for the smallest body size practical

claims.note: Compare rp2350.decoupling.per_pin and rp2350.decoupling.dvdd, which fix 100 nF per IOVDD/DVDD pin as datasheet requirements. Those are chip-specific and not contradicted here, but this claim would argue that e.g. 1 uF 0402 is no worse at high frequency. Chip-vendor values win for package checks.

claims.statement: When high-frequency decoupling is poor, reduce the capacitance so the capacitor's series self-resonance lands on the offending frequency; a larger value does not help.

citations.quote: When poor decoupling of high frequencies is suspected, decrease the value of capacitance (or preferably, do the homework and look up the series self-resonance).

claims.note: Valid for narrow-band RF rejection with high-Q C0G parts; disputed for broadband digital PDNs with MLCCs whose ESL is independent of value (bogatin_myth3).

claims.statement: Each decoupling capacitor's mounting loop inductance (excluding its own ESL) is held under a budget, 0.7-1 nH in TI's OMAP4430 example, read at 50 MHz; power/ground plane pairs near the capacitor's surface reduce it.

citations.locator: §3 p.9, Table 5, last column 'Maximum loop inductance per capacitor (without ESL) (nH)'
citations.quote: VCORE1_OMAP_MPU 1GHz 93 40 14 0.7
Typically, capacitors loop inductance is determined at a frequency of 50 MHz.
Placing power and ground plane pairs closer to the surface where the capacitor is mounted.

claims.could_enforce: loop inductance estimate from cap pads + via geometry + plane spacing (fast-tier formula from SLOA069 p.10-11, or slow-tier field solve)
claims.note: Numbers are OMAP4430-specific; no RP2350 budget is published. On a 2-layer 1.6 mm board one via alone is ~1 nH (SLOA069 p.11), so the budget is unreachable without short paths to an adjacent plane.

claims.statement: Rail impedance stays below Ztarget = V_rail x ripple_fraction / (0.5 x I_max_transient) from DC to the specified frequency; a resonant peak below that frequency means changing or adding capacitor values.

citations.quote: the objective is to maintain the target spectrum below the Z target value (Ztarget) from DC to Fmax
If resonant peak appears before the required decoupling frequency then the decoupling strategy should be modified
keep the impedance profile, as seen by the pads of the IC, a flat impedance and at a value that is acceptably low

claims.could_enforce: slow-tier: AC sweep of the extracted PDN against Z_target (needs I_transient from the chip package)
claims.note: SWPA222 also sets an IR-drop allowance of 0.5-2.5 % of nominal voltage (§2 p.4).
